title: Narrowing down a bug
summary: When there is no error to read, reproduce the bug, cut the system in half, and let git bisect find the commit that broke it.
youWillLearn: How to turn "it's broken sometimes" into steps that fail every time
How to isolate a bug by testing one half of the system at a time
Binary search with log probes inside your own code
How git bisect finds the exact commit that broke something

glossary.app server: A computer that runs the app's own code and answers the browser. While you build, it runs on your laptop.
glossary.reproduce: To find exact steps that make the bug happen every time you follow them.
glossary.isolate: To test one part of the system on its own, so a result can only be explained by that part.
glossary.curl: A command-line tool that sends one request to a server, exactly as written, without a browser.
glossary.binary search: Finding something by checking the middle, keeping the half that contains it, and repeating. Each check halves what is left.
glossary.probe: A temporary log line placed at one point in the code to check whether the data is still correct there.
glossary.commit: A saved snapshot of the code in git, with an id like 9f2e1aa and a message describing the change.
glossary.git bisect: A git command that runs a binary search through your commits to find the first one where a bug appears.
glossary.regression: A bug in something that used to work, brought in by a later change.

steps.title: Notely's Summarize button, last week
body: Last week, Notely's Summarize button worked. Maya's browser (the screen she uses) asks the app server, the computer running Notely's code.
The app server loads the note from the database (where notes are kept), sends its text to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, and sends a three-line summary back to the browser.

scene.caption: The browser asks the app server, which uses the database and the Claude API.

steps.title: Blank summaries, and no error anywhere
body: Since sometime this week, summaries come back blank. The Console is empty, Network shows 200 (success), and the server logs show no errors.
With nothing to read, the last three lessons point nowhere. The bug could be in the page, the app server, the database or the Claude call. You need a method, not a guess.
changes: ~ Browser shows a blank summary
~ App Server, Database and Claude API: all suspects
~ Suspects 0 → 4

scene.caption: No errors anywhere. Every part of Notely is a suspect.

steps.title: Shrink the haystack, half at a time
body: Do not search for the bug. Search for where it is not. Pick a test whose answer rules out a big part of the system, ideally half.
Each test cuts the suspects down. A handful of good tests corners almost any bug, even in code you did not write yourself, which with Claude Code is often the case.

callout.text: A string of fairy lights goes dark. You do not test every bulb. You check the middle of the string: power there? Then the fault is in the second half. Check its middle. Repeat.

changes: + Two halves: the page, and the server side

scene.caption: One test at the right point clears half the suspects at once.

steps.title: Step one: make it fail on demand
body: A bug you cannot reproduce is a bug you cannot prove fixed. Write down the exact steps, and vary one thing at a time: another note, another user, your laptop instead of the live site.
It fails for every note and every user, on your laptop too. So it is not one odd note, and you can test locally.

code.code:
1. Log in as maya@example.com (local or live)
2. Open any note, e.g. n_81
3. Click "Summarize"
Expected: 3-line summary
Actual:   empty box, status 200, no error
Since:    worked last Monday

changes: ~ Browser: fails for every note, locally too
~ Tests run 0 → 1

scene.caption: A reliable repro: every note, every user, on your laptop too.

steps.title: Isolate: skip the page entirely
body: Now isolate: test the server side without the page. From the terminal, call the app server directly with curl, a tool that sends one request. If the raw answer is already wrong, the page is innocent.
It is: the answer is {}, an empty object, with no summary at all. The page was faithfully showing nothing.

code.caption: If the route needs a login, add your local cookie with -H "Cookie: …". Never share that command.

changes: + Terminal: sends the request without the page
~ Outlines go; App Server answers {}: the page is cleared
~ Suspects 4 → 3
~ Tests run 1 → 2

scene.caption: Called directly, the app server already answers an empty object. The page is cleared.

steps.title: Binary search inside the app server
body: The summary code has three stages: load the note, call Claude, build the reply. Put a probe in the middle: log the raw Claude answer, then run the same curl.
The answer holds a full summary. Loading and calling work; the bug is in the last stage. That is binary search: test the middle, keep the bad half.

code.caption: Mark probes with PROBE so they are easy to find. This one prints note content: run it locally only and delete it before committing.

changes: − Browser, Terminal, Database, Claude API, App Server: we zoom in
+ Load note, Call Claude, Build reply: the code's three stages
~ Suspects 3 → 1
~ Tests run 2 → 3

scene.caption: A probe after the Claude call shows good data, so the bug is in building the reply.

steps.title: git bisect: binary search through time
body: The reply code looks fine, yet it worked last Monday. So a later commit (a saved version of the code) broke it, a regression. Git bisect finds it.
Name a good commit and a bad one. Git switches to the one halfway between; test it and say good or bad. 100 commits take about 7 tests.

code.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # the current commit is broken
git bisect good a1b2c3d     # last Monday's commit worked
# git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then:
git bisect good             # or: git bisect bad
# ...repeat until git prints "is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset            # back to where you started
code.caption: If a script can tell good from bad, git bisect run <script> does the testing for you.

changes: − Load note, Call Claude, Build reply
+ Commits a1b2c3d, 5d0e7b2, c48f019, 9f2e1aa, e77a3d4
~ Commits left – → 4: any one after Monday

scene.caption: The commits since Monday, oldest first. Git checks out the middle one for you to test.

steps.title: The first bad commit, found
body: c48f019 works: mark it good. Git jumps to 9f2e1aa. Blank summary: mark it bad. Git prints 9f2e1aa is the first bad commit, "refactor summary types".
Its diff is tiny. The refactor reads .value, a field the Claude API never sends. An undefined value silently drops out of JSON, so the app server sent {}.

code.caption: SummaryBlock said value, but the API sends text. as SummaryBlock told TypeScript, the type checker, to trust that wrong shape, so nothing warned.

changes: ~ c48f019 tests good; 5d0e7b2 before it is good too
~ 9f2e1aa tests bad: the first bad commit
~ Tests run 3 → 5
~ Commits left 4 → 1

scene.caption: Two tests later, git names the first bad commit: 9f2e1aa.

steps.title: Change one thing, then test
body: Narrowing only works if each test changes one thing. Edit three files, restart, and it works? You no longer know which edit fixed it, or whether one of them broke something else.
Same while bisecting: no fixes until git has named the commit. Then run git bisect reset, make the fix on today's code, and re-run the repro steps.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code to reproduce first, then propose one change and say what result would prove it right. Check git diff --stat: a one-line bug deserves a small diff. And ask it to remove every PROBE line before committing.

changes: + Fix: one line on top of today's code
~ e77a3d4 back in view: the fix builds on it

scene.caption: One small fix on top of today's code, tested with the same repro steps.

steps.title: Recap: a method beats a hunch
body: Reproduce until it fails every time. Isolate by testing one half of the system, like calling the app server without the page. Binary search inside the code with probes.
When it used to work, let git bisect find the first bad commit. Change one thing per test, and prove the fix with the same repro steps.
changes: ~ Fix passes the repro steps: summaries are back
~ Suspects 1 → 0

scene.caption: The same repro that showed the bug now passes.

quiz.question: A client says bookings "sometimes" fail. You cannot make it happen. What is the best first move?

options.text: Ask Claude Code to add retries to every database call.
options.why: That guesses at a cause you have not found, and may hide the real one.

options.text: Collect exact cases: which user, which time slot, which device, and what they saw.
options.why: "Sometimes" usually means "under conditions we have not noticed yet". Finding them is how you get a reliable repro.

options.text: Rewrite the booking flow, since it is clearly fragile.
options.why: A rewrite without knowing the cause can carry the same bug over, and you cannot prove it is gone.

quiz.question: The page shows a wrong price. You call the app server with curl and the price in its answer is correct. What have you learned?

options.text: The bug is on the server side, in how the price is calculated.
options.why: The server sent the right price, so its calculation is fine.

options.text: Nothing, since curl and the browser behave differently.
options.why: The server's answer does not depend on who asks, unless login or headers differ. A matching request is a fair test.

options.text: The bug is in the page: how it reads or displays the price.
options.why: The server half is cleared. Whatever goes wrong happens after the answer arrives in the browser.

quiz.question: A feature worked 120 commits ago and is broken now. Roughly how many tests does git bisect need to find the first bad commit?

options.why: Each test halves the range: 120, 60, 30, 15, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is about 7 tests.
That would be a straight walk through history. Bisect jumps to the middle each time instead.
Testing every commit is exactly the slow path bisect saves you from.

takeaways: First reproduce: exact steps that fail every time. Without them you cannot prove a fix.
Isolate by testing one half of the system, for example curl the app server to skip the page.
Inside the code, place a PROBE log in the middle and keep the half where the data goes wrong.
When it used to work, git bisect finds the first bad commit in a handful of tests.
Change one thing per test, and remove probes before you commit.
